news.summaryTr: While many people find a diagnosis for ADHD or autism affirming, a government-funded clinic in Sweden is re-assessing people who feel it does not reflect them.
news.articleText: A clinic is reassessing people with ADHD and autism diagnoses - but critics fear it could deepen stigma - Published Freya looks nervous as she walks into a psychiatric clinic in Sweden for an ADHD assessment. Countries around the world have seen a huge increase in ADHD diagnoses over recent decades. For many people this can be life changing, helping them understand themselves better and access support. But Freya (not her real name) is not attending a long-awaited appointment to secure a diagnosis. This government-funded clinic offers autism and ADHD diagnosis reassessments - its doctors believe it is the first in the world dedicated solely to this purpose. At 12, Freya was struggling with anxiety at school and sought out professional help. "They thought I had ADHD," she says. But as she grew up, she felt that she did not experience ADHD symptoms. "I don't think I had it in the first place," she now says. Her doubts about the diagnosis became more pressing as a teenager, when she discovered that in Sweden, it could be a barrier to pursuing her dream career of joining the police. "I want to have every option open," she tells BBC World Service. If the doctors at the clinic decide Freya does not meet the ADHD criteria, her medical records will be updated, and it will be easier for her to apply for a job with the police. The clinic, known as Mottagning Neuropsykiatri, has opened at a time when rates of ADHD and autism diagnoses are under the spotlight. Many say this is because of greater awareness of the symptoms, and that previously neglected groups - particularly women and girls - are finally getting the diagnoses they need, while others argue that the growing numbers stem from overdiagnosis. The existence of the clinic is controversial. Clinical guidance from UK governing bodies and the World Health Organization describe autism as a lifelong condition and ADHD as a neurodevelopmental condition that can persist into adulthood. The medical consensus is that both diagnoses last a lifetime, even if symptoms fluctuate. And some neurodiversity advocates warn that a dedicated reassessment service could reinforce the idea that being diagnosed with ADHD or autism is undesirable – and deepen the stigma surrounding both conditions. Despite this, hundreds of people have approached the clinic about reassessment. Barred from jobs Like Freya, other young adults have been prompted to reconsider their diagnosis after they felt it had become a barrier. This is because historically, Swedes with ADHD or autism were barred from certain jobs, including joining the military, and becoming police officers, train drivers and pilots. This is despite research suggesting some neurodivergent traits can be strengths in certain roles. No such bans exist in the UK, although rules differ globally. Since 2022, people with ADHD have been able to join the Swedish military if they are medication-free. And since 2021, people with ADHD or autism have been able to apply to join the police, but must submit a medical certificate, which can cost around 15,000 SEK (£1,100) privately. When Freya was referred to the clinic, she says she was relieved to find out she could get her diagnosis reassessed there for free. Johanna, 24, was diagnosed with ADHD at 14 after what she describes as a period of bad behaviour at school. She found the diagnosis helpful at first and received additional support from teachers. But as she grew into adulthood, she says she stopped feeling that she needed extra support. And after discovering it was a barrier to becoming a police officer, she began questioning whether it was even accurate. Johanna says she has some traits of ADHD, such as a short attention span, "but not enough to have an ADHD diagnosis," she believes. Johanna was reassessed aged 21 during an early pilot of the reassessment clinic and was found not to meet its diagnostic criteria for ADHD. She now works for her father's company, and does not plan on becoming a police officer. What is an ADHD or autism reassessment? Both ADHD and autism are neurodevelopmental conditions that affect how people think and interact with the world. They are diagnosed through detailed assessments, which can include questionnaires and interviews, rather than one single clinical test. The doctors at Mottagning Neuropsykiatri say their approach is different from traditional assessments, as it focuses less on someone's history, and more on the symptoms they are experiencing in the present. "This is not de-diagnosing, this is a renewed assessment of your functioning today," says Sebastian Lundström, the clinic's lead psychologist. The doctors say they do not judge whether the original assessment was correct, so rather than wiping the original diagnosis from patients' medical records, they add a note of the new assessment. Lundström says that some people who once had a diagnosis but are found to not meet the criteria at the clinic may have been misdiagnosed. But he also believes that for a small minority, ADHD and autism are not lifelong conditions and individuals may stop experiencing symptoms as they grow older. But updating a person's diagnosis because they are not currently showing symptoms is a contested approach. "We have to remember that these are lifelong conditions," says Navid Ghannad, chair of Autism Skåne, a local Swedish non-profit for autistic people and their families. "Because at a certain point in their adulthood during a clinical setting they have had their diagnosis removed, it doesn't necessarily mean that the ADHD or the autism has disappeared," he adds. Symptoms could reappear later in life, he says. "The problem is once they resurface, that individual which doesn't have a diagnosis any longer, they will not be able to get the timely and correct support." Lundström says he does not consider it a big risk that people could get reassessed and find themselves without necessary support. During the pilot he encountered people who "really wanted" to get rid of their diagnosis but the psychologist said, "we still feel that you meet the criteria". 'I was stuck' Vilda, 22, sought reassessment of her autism diagnosis which was initially given after she experienced a trauma. "I didn't recognise myself in the description of autism," she says. "I was stuck. I know that this is not me, but I can't do anything about it." It was requests from people like Johanna and Vilda that led to the establishment of the clinic, Lundström explains. "It gained momentum by itself and the word spread around. A lot of people contacted us and we felt that there was a justification for starting up," he says. It is only open one day a month. Before opening the clinic, Lundström conducted a small peer-reviewed study - of the 72 individuals who took part, roughly 80% did not meet the criteria for ADHD or autism. All the participants already wanted to lose their diagnosis, rather than being a randomly selected group. "It's important to stress that this patient population is not necessarily representative for all with autism and ADHD," he adds. During the first year of the pilot some 400 to 500 people spoke to Lundström, who is also associate professor of child and adolescent psychiatric sciences at the University of Gothenburg, about getting a reassessment. The project also has the backing of senior figures in Swedish psychiatry, including Sophia Eberhard, a senior consultant specialising in child and adolescent psychiatry. "It's psychiatry who in the beginning made those diagnoses," she says. "I believe we have a responsibility to help these young adults on their way." In September, the BBC was given permission to join Freya as she became the first patient to attend the newly opened clinic, which serves both men and women. During her appointment, Freya takes part in questionnaires and verbal assessments to see if she meets the ADHD criteria. The process is the same for both ADHD and autism, although the questions differ. Freya says she is hopeful that she will be able to "get rid" of her ADHD diagnosis after the appointment. But the doctors are adamant that they do not just give attendees the outcome they want. They conduct other checks such as assessing body language and communication skills, speaking to younger patients' parents, and checking medical files for ongoing treatment. Fears about stigma The opening of the clinic has drawn criticism from those who fear it sends the wrong message about autism and ADHD. "The clinic presents neurodiversity and autistic people as a bad thing, like we are a problem that needs to be fixed - we are not," says Jenny Hedin, from charity Organiserade Autister Västernorrland, an advocacy organisation run by and for autistic adults. Hedin, who is autistic and has ADHD, warns that people who can successfully "mask" or mimic neurotypical behaviour might feel under pressure to lose their diagnosis in order to be better accepted by society. "That is especially a problem with women and girls, because girls are usually great at masking," she adds. Others say the focus should be on changing the rules that make it difficult for people with ADHD or autism to pursue certain careers. Eric Donell, the chairman of Riksförbundet Attention, a national Swedish charity, lobbies to remove employment restrictions affecting neurodivergent people, which he says are unfair. He stresses that for many people, getting a diagnosis is extremely important. "Instead of asking people to get rid of their diagnosis, sometimes we should just ask whether the rules themselves are justified," he says. Reassessments risk becoming "a way of adapting the individual to society instead of adapting society to human differences," he adds. 'Magic spell' People from the UK, Denmark, Norway and Germany have also been in touch for reassessment, says Lundström, but they have been turned away, as the clinic only serves locals. Georgina, 35, from the UK, contacted the clinic because she wants to have the autism diagnosis she received at 25 "removed". "It felt like a magic spell, that I'd get this label and the world would be more understanding," she says. Instead, she says, her colleagues belittled her. Georgina has since been offered an NHS reassessment. The process is the same as the original assessment she went through, and can result in patients receiving more diagnoses, fewer diagnoses or no change. The Swedish reassessment clinic says they generally would not apply new or additional diagnoses to people - something Georgina was attracted to. "The situation where you can go in and then come out with other labels... that's really off-putting," she says. For now, she has decided not to undergo an NHS reassessment. Instead, she is trying to find out how often a diagnosis is reconsidered, before deciding whether to go ahead. Back in Sweden, a few hours after Freya entered the clinic, she re-emerges from a consultation room. The doctors here have found that, right now, she does not meet the criteria for an ADHD diagnosis. She says it is "confirmation" that she was right to question her diagnosis. "Now, finally, I have the same opportunity as everyone else."

news.summary: China's immense clout now also has the flex of soft power. Critics and dissidents say their voices are being drowned out.

news.titleTr: Behind China's spectacular rise, voices who defied it say they are being drowned out
news.summaryTr: China's immense clout now also has the flex of soft power. Critics and dissidents say their voices are being drowned out.
news.articleText: Behind China's spectacular rise, voices who defied it say they are being drowned out - Published For Uyghur activist Dolkun Isa, who has lived in exile in Germany for nearly three decades, the thinning of the crowds is the clearest measure of how much his cause is slipping off the world's radar. "Back in 2018, we could easily get thousands of people out in the streets to protest against China's human rights violations. Nowadays, we have trouble finding even 500." It was in 2018 that reports emerged that China had detained up to a million Uyghurs and other Muslims in mass internment camps in its north-western province of Xinjiang. Beijing, which said the camps were for "re-education" to counter separatist violence, denied the allegations detailing alarming rights abuses. But an international outcry, including protests, followed. Western governments rolled out trade bans and sanctions against senior Chinese officials, and froze their assets, and at least nine countries issued parliamentary resolutions condemning the detentions. It was a time "when we felt the world was finally listening", says Dolkun, 59, who served as president of the Munich-based World Uyghur Congress from 2017-2024 . But today, "we find ourselves competing against economic interests and geopolitical calculations to capture the world's attention. For me, this is one of the most painful aspects of our struggle". Few corners of the world remain untouched by China's rise. Its electric vehicles pack highways from Brazil to Belgium, made-in-China batteries, solar panels, AI models and microdramas fuel daily consumption in so many places, and Labubu dolls, Pop Mart's furry gap-toothed plush, dangle from backpacks almost everywhere. China's immense economic clout now also has the flex of soft power, drowning out voices that say their fight against the Communist Party cannot compete with the country's gleaming skylines, advanced exports or futuristic ambitions. Buoyed by its successes, Beijing is also swapping the "stick" for the "carrot", says Uyghur journalist Arslan Hidayat, who was born and raised in Australia, where he runs Kashgar Times. Activists tell the BBC Beijing has been offering family reunions, money and the promise of safety - in return, they are asked for information about their networks and to promote pro-party narratives. The result, activists say, is a movement with fewer voices and less trust. The Chinese embassy in the UK dismissed the activists' claims that they would be asked to spy on or disclose information about fellow exiles. China's "economic muscle" has earned it respect abroad and reshaped foreign policy, says Ian Johnson, a Pulitzer Prize-winning journalist who has long reported on Chinese civil society. "At the same time, Western governments have become much more inwardly focused and populist, pushing human rights down their lists of priorities." China's human rights record has not earned a mention in any of the three summits Xi Jinping and US President Donald Trump held this year, including the one in Shenzhen last week. As Beijing's leverage on the global stage has grown, so has the cost of confrontation or condemnation. This shift in Beijing's image and tactics is deeply worrying, dissidents say, because it is weakening both their networks and the international pressure they hope to build. In July Tibetan activist Lobga Rangzen died after he set himself on fire outside the UN headquarters in New York. He was protesting against China's sweeping new "ethnic unity law" which, among other things, requires minorities, including Tibetans, to learn Mandarin. The UN called it an "absolutely tragic" incident, but attention quickly faded. His death was "an appeal to the international community", says Tenzin Dorjee, a researcher at the Tibet Action Institute, but he thinks much of the world is reluctant to criticise China because of the power it wields. That same month Dolkun tried to rally supporters against the same law but he met with a muted response. "Many people have dialled down on their activism over the years because they are thinking about their loved ones back in China," Dolkun says. Arslan says he has interviewed at least a dozen Uyghur exiles who were "invited to go back to China on the condition that they would provide information to Chinese agents from time to time". The questions seem "fairly innocuous", he adds: "Who lives around you? Which Uyghur restaurants do you frequent? We believe these are used to build out the profiles of dissidents overseas." Beijing's embassy in the UK said in its response to the BBC that "facilitating visits to China by overseas Chinese to reunite with their families" is a "normal part" of consular services. "China respects and protects the lawful rights and interests of people of all ethnic groups, including the Uyghurs, and their freedom to maintain contact with family members overseas," it added. These family visits often happen in large groups and are well documented on China's official platforms. In Turkey, which hosts tens of thousands of Muslim minorities from Xinjiang, Chinese Consul-General Wei Xiaodong was photographed sending off some 30 participants from Istanbul in January. "He expressed hope that the diaspora returning to Xinjiang would experience the region's development... and would actively promote these developments upon their return to Turkey," read a post on the consulate's WeChat page. Beijing has repackaged Xinjiang into a traveller's haven. The region saw more than 300 million domestic and international tourist visits last year, more than double the number in 2018, Chinese authorities say. The post from China's Turkish consulate concluded with a clip showing loved ones hugging and presenting bouquets as they reunite with family at the airport in Urumqi, the capital of Xinjiang. "People are happy to stay quiet and lay low for the little communication they've been allowed to establish with their loved ones," Arslan says. Though the trips are publicised, it is unclear what makes someone eligible to participate in them. Some suggest that even dating histories come under the microscope. Alim*, a Uyghur exiled in Turkey, says a friend who made an appeal to the consulate to consider her for a trip was rejected, with staffers alluding to her past relationship with a Kazakh man who at one point was "quite active" in lobbying for his parents who were detained in China. "She was very eager to go on one of these 'family visits' because she hasn't seen her loved ones back home in so many years... She was crushed that she was rejected," says Alim. "The way I understand it, the 'ideal participant' is someone influential enough to amplify China's messages, yet not associated with anything or anyone too political." When Mehmut* was invited on a family visit in October 2024, he jumped at the opportunity. The Uyghur businessman hoped a trip back to China would help him re-establish the links needed to "keep our business afloat". Far from the warm reunions Mehmut had expected, he says his engagement with friends and family "felt superficial". "It was not like officials were actively monitoring me or restricting my movements. But there was a great dose of fear and self-censorship in my conversations with people," he says. "Some were caught off guard to see me return, others appeared very cautious with what they told me. The experience just made me feel very uncomfortable." These visits do not just serve Beijing's narrative; they also drive a wedge within communities, activists say. Abduweli Ayup, a prominent Uyghur linguist based in Norway, has observed former activists going off the grid after returning from these trips. "Some have deleted their social media accounts and cut off contact with us," he says. "Others appear to be suspicious of us or concerned that what we were doing would compromise theirs or their families' safety." The fact that only a few get selected to visit the homeland "creates confusion within the diaspora," says Tibetan activist Karma Rinchen. "They get sidelined when they return... Very sadly, our suspicions that some of them are feeding information back to the Chinese authorities have turned out to be true." Rinchen serves as information secretary in the Tibetan government-in-exile in the northern Indian town of Dharamshala. His parents were among thousands who followed their spiritual leader Dalai Lama into exile after China annexed Tibet. Over the decades, waves of others have fled Chinese rule seeking greater freedom or asylum from Beijing's crackdowns - dissidents and student activists in the wake of the Tiannanmen Square massacre; lawyers, journalists, purged officials and critics in the years after, and, more recently, Hong Kong saw a steady exodus build as the pro-democracy movement was crushed. Many have kept on fighting. But now, they say, Beijing's might is chipping away at their struggle, making it ever harder to stand up to the Chinese Communist Party. "Many among us have been separated from our families for generations and are eager to set foot on Tibet soil," Rinchen says. "This is exactly the kind of desperation the Communist Party seeks to target." But he adds this only means communities have to "work harder to make sure their voices are heard". "For Tibetans, this is not something we can simply walk away from. Our struggle is about our identity, our culture, our religion and the basic rights of our people. We have been doing this work for many decades, and we have learned to remain patient and persistent," Rinchen adds. For many, that persistence continues to be tested on a personal level. Uyghur musician Mirkamel Tourghoun has lived as a refugee in Paris since 2008, spending most of his time writing music and making films about Uyghur culture. The 42-year-old has chosen the painful path of cutting off contact with his family who remain in Urumqi. In January, he received a call from someone claiming to be an official from the city. "What if we get rid of all this [political] pressure, and allow you to return and see your parents? Do you have such plans?" the caller asked. "What's happened in the past is in the past. You should turn a new page. The pen is in your own hand." The official claimed his father was gravely ill and that time was running out to see him. "It's emotional blackmail," Mirkamel says. He declined the official's invitation: "Tell my family to forget they ever had a child like me. There is no other solution." * Name changed on request to protect interviewee's identity
news.articleTextTr: Behind China's spectacular rise, voices who defied it say they are being drowned out - Published For Uyghur activist Dolkun Isa, who has lived in exile in Germany for nearly three decades, the thinning of the crowds is the clearest measure of how much his cause is slipping off the world's radar. "Back in 2018, we could easily get thousands of people out in the streets to protest against China's human rights violations. Nowadays, we have trouble finding even 500." It was in 2018 that reports emerged that China had detained up to a million Uyghurs and other Muslims in mass internment camps in its north-western province of Xinjiang. Beijing, which said the camps were for "re-education" to counter separatist violence, denied the allegations detailing alarming rights abuses. But an international outcry, including protests, followed. Western governments rolled out trade bans and sanctions against senior Chinese officials, and froze their assets, and at least nine countries issued parliamentary resolutions condemning the detentions. It was a time "when we felt the world was finally listening", says Dolkun, 59, who served as president of the Munich-based World Uyghur Congress from 2017-2024 . But today, "we find ourselves competing against economic interests and geopolitical calculations to capture the world's attention. For me, this is one of the most painful aspects of our struggle". Few corners of the world remain untouched by China's rise. Its electric vehicles pack highways from Brazil to Belgium, made-in-China batteries, solar panels, AI models and microdramas fuel daily consumption in so many places, and Labubu dolls, Pop Mart's furry gap-toothed plush, dangle from backpacks almost everywhere. China's immense economic clout now also has the flex of soft power, drowning out voices that say their fight against the Communist Party cannot compete with the country's gleaming skylines, advanced exports or futuristic ambitions. Buoyed by its successes, Beijing is also swapping the "stick" for the "carrot", says Uyghur journalist Arslan Hidayat, who was born and raised in Australia, where he runs Kashgar Times. Activists tell the BBC Beijing has been offering family reunions, money and the promise of safety - in return, they are asked for information about their networks and to promote pro-party narratives. The result, activists say, is a movement with fewer voices and less trust. The Chinese embassy in the UK dismissed the activists' claims that they would be asked to spy on or disclose information about fellow exiles. China's "economic muscle" has earned it respect abroad and reshaped foreign policy, says Ian Johnson, a Pulitzer Prize-winning journalist who has long reported on Chinese civil society. "At the same time, Western governments have become much more inwardly focused and populist, pushing human rights down their lists of priorities." China's human rights record has not earned a mention in any of the three summits Xi Jinping and US President Donald Trump held this year, including the one in Shenzhen last week. As Beijing's leverage on the global stage has grown, so has the cost of confrontation or condemnation. This shift in Beijing's image and tactics is deeply worrying, dissidents say, because it is weakening both their networks and the international pressure they hope to build. In July Tibetan activist Lobga Rangzen died after he set himself on fire outside the UN headquarters in New York. He was protesting against China's sweeping new "ethnic unity law" which, among other things, requires minorities, including Tibetans, to learn Mandarin. The UN called it an "absolutely tragic" incident, but attention quickly faded. His death was "an appeal to the international community", says Tenzin Dorjee, a researcher at the Tibet Action Institute, but he thinks much of the world is reluctant to criticise China because of the power it wields. That same month Dolkun tried to rally supporters against the same law but he met with a muted response. "Many people have dialled down on their activism over the years because they are thinking about their loved ones back in China," Dolkun says. Arslan says he has interviewed at least a dozen Uyghur exiles who were "invited to go back to China on the condition that they would provide information to Chinese agents from time to time". The questions seem "fairly innocuous", he adds: "Who lives around you? Which Uyghur restaurants do you frequent? We believe these are used to build out the profiles of dissidents overseas." Beijing's embassy in the UK said in its response to the BBC that "facilitating visits to China by overseas Chinese to reunite with their families" is a "normal part" of consular services. "China respects and protects the lawful rights and interests of people of all ethnic groups, including the Uyghurs, and their freedom to maintain contact with family members overseas," it added. These family visits often happen in large groups and are well documented on China's official platforms. In Turkey, which hosts tens of thousands of Muslim minorities from Xinjiang, Chinese Consul-General Wei Xiaodong was photographed sending off some 30 participants from Istanbul in January. "He expressed hope that the diaspora returning to Xinjiang would experience the region's development... and would actively promote these developments upon their return to Turkey," read a post on the consulate's WeChat page. Beijing has repackaged Xinjiang into a traveller's haven. The region saw more than 300 million domestic and international tourist visits last year, more than double the number in 2018, Chinese authorities say. The post from China's Turkish consulate concluded with a clip showing loved ones hugging and presenting bouquets as they reunite with family at the airport in Urumqi, the capital of Xinjiang. "People are happy to stay quiet and lay low for the little communication they've been allowed to establish with their loved ones," Arslan says. Though the trips are publicised, it is unclear what makes someone eligible to participate in them. Some suggest that even dating histories come under the microscope. Alim*, a Uyghur exiled in Turkey, says a friend who made an appeal to the consulate to consider her for a trip was rejected, with staffers alluding to her past relationship with a Kazakh man who at one point was "quite active" in lobbying for his parents who were detained in China. "She was very eager to go on one of these 'family visits' because she hasn't seen her loved ones back home in so many years... She was crushed that she was rejected," says Alim. "The way I understand it, the 'ideal participant' is someone influential enough to amplify China's messages, yet not associated with anything or anyone too political." When Mehmut* was invited on a family visit in October 2024, he jumped at the opportunity. The Uyghur businessman hoped a trip back to China would help him re-establish the links needed to "keep our business afloat". Far from the warm reunions Mehmut had expected, he says his engagement with friends and family "felt superficial". "It was not like officials were actively monitoring me or restricting my movements. But there was a great dose of fear and self-censorship in my conversations with people," he says. "Some were caught off guard to see me return, others appeared very cautious with what they told me. The experience just made me feel very uncomfortable." These visits do not just serve Beijing's narrative; they also drive a wedge within communities, activists say. Abduweli Ayup, a prominent Uyghur linguist based in Norway, has observed former activists going off the grid after returning from these trips. "Some have deleted their social media accounts and cut off contact with us," he says. "Others appear to be suspicious of us or concerned that what we were doing would compromise theirs or their families' safety." The fact that only a few get selected to visit the homeland "creates confusion within the diaspora," says Tibetan activist Karma Rinchen. "They get sidelined when they return... Very sadly, our suspicions that some of them are feeding information back to the Chinese authorities have turned out to be true." Rinchen serves as information secretary in the Tibetan government-in-exile in the northern Indian town of Dharamshala. His parents were among thousands who followed their spiritual leader Dalai Lama into exile after China annexed Tibet. Over the decades, waves of others have fled Chinese rule seeking greater freedom or asylum from Beijing's crackdowns - dissidents and student activists in the wake of the Tiannanmen Square massacre; lawyers, journalists, purged officials and critics in the years after, and, more recently, Hong Kong saw a steady exodus build as the pro-democracy movement was crushed. Many have kept on fighting. But now, they say, Beijing's might is chipping away at their struggle, making it ever harder to stand up to the Chinese Communist Party. "Many among us have been separated from our families for generations and are eager to set foot on Tibet soil," Rinchen says. "This is exactly the kind of desperation the Communist Party seeks to target." But he adds this only means communities have to "work harder to make sure their voices are heard". "For Tibetans, this is not something we can simply walk away from. Our struggle is about our identity, our culture, our religion and the basic rights of our people. We have been doing this work for many decades, and we have learned to remain patient and persistent," Rinchen adds. For many, that persistence continues to be tested on a personal level. Uyghur musician Mirkamel Tourghoun has lived as a refugee in Paris since 2008, spending most of his time writing music and making films about Uyghur culture. The 42-year-old has chosen the painful path of cutting off contact with his family who remain in Urumqi. In January, he received a call from someone claiming to be an official from the city. "What if we get rid of all this [political] pressure, and allow you to return and see your parents? Do you have such plans?" the caller asked. "What's happened in the past is in the past. You should turn a new page. The pen is in your own hand." The official claimed his father was gravely ill and that time was running out to see him. "It's emotional blackmail," Mirkamel says. He declined the official's invitation: "Tell my family to forget they ever had a child like me. There is no other solution." * Name changed on request to protect interviewee's identity

news.articleText: Altın için devi uyandıran tahmin: Uzman isim tarih ve fiyat için son noktayı koydu J.P. Morgan stratejisti Yuxuan Tang, ons altının 2027 sonunda 4.600 dolara ulaşabileceğini öngördü. Bankaya göre yüksek tahvil getirileri kısa vadede baskı yaratırken doların zayıflaması ve merkez bankalarının alımları 2027'nin ikinci yarısında altını destekleyebilir. J.P. Morgan'dan altın için 4.600 dolar tahmini J.P. Morgan stratejisti Yuxuan Tang, ons altının 2027 sonunda 4.600 dolara ulaşabileceğini söyledi. CNBC'ye konuşan Tang, bankanın önümüzdeki bir yıllık dönemde altın fiyatında yaklaşık yüzde 30 yükseliş beklediğini belirtti. Yüksek tahvil getirileri kısa vadede baskı yaratabilir Tang, ABD'de para politikasındaki sıkılaşmanın ve yükselen tahvil getirilerinin kısa vadede altın fiyatlarını baskılayabileceğini ifade etti. Faiz getirisi olmayan altının bu dönemde daha güçlü tahvil getirileriyle rekabet etmesi bekleniyor. Güçlü dolar görünümü 3-6 ay daha sürebilir ABD ekonomisinin dirençli seyri ve yapay zeka yatırımlarının ülkeye çektiği sermaye doların gücünü destekliyor. Tang, güçlü dolar görünümünün üç ila altı ay daha devam edebileceğini söyledi. Altın için dönüm noktası 2027'nin ikinci yarısı Tang'a göre Fed'in 2027'nin ikinci çeyreğinin ardından nötr para politikası duruşuna geçmesi ve likidite koşullarının iyileşmesi, altın fiyatları için daha elverişli bir ortam oluşturabilir. Doların zayıflaması altına destek verebilir J.P. Morgan'ın modeline göre dolar, uzun vadeli ortalamasının yaklaşık yüzde 10 üzerinde bulunuyor. Tang, uluslararası yatırımcıların portföylerindeki dolar ağırlığını azaltmasıyla ABD para biriminin 2027'nin ikinci yarısında yeniden zayıflamasını bekliyor. Merkez bankalarının altın alımları sürebilir Tang, rezervlerini çeşitlendirmek isteyen merkez bankalarının altın alımlarını sürdürmesini bekliyor. Merkez bankalarının talebi, orta vadede altın fiyatlarını destekleyebilecek unsurlar arasında gösteriliyor. Para birimlerindeki değer kaybı altına talebi artırabilir Para birimlerinin değer kaybına karşı korunmak isteyen yatırımcıların da altına yönelmesi bekleniyor. Tang'a göre bu eğilim, orta vadede altın fiyatlarına destek sağlayabilir. Ons altın cuma günü yüzde 1,31 yükseldi Kitco'nun haberine göre spot altının ons fiyatı cuma günü 3.685,30 dolara kadar yükseldi. Haber yayımlandığı sırada günlük yüzde 1,31 artışla 3.640,36 dolardan işlem görüyordu.

news.titleTr: Kamuda 49 sayfalık kadro düzenlemesi: Bakanlıklar ve kritik kurumlarda değişiklik
news.summaryTr: Adalet, Aile ve Sosyal Hizmetler, Sağlık, Hazine ve Maliye ile İçişleri bakanlıklarının da aralarında bulunduğu çok sayıda kamu kurumunun dolu ve boş kadrolarında değişikliğe gidildi. 49 sayfalık Cumhurbaşkanı Kararı, kadroların unvan ve derece cetvellerini yeniden düzenliyor.
news.articleText: Kamuda 49 sayfalık kadro düzenlemesi: Bakanlıklar ve kritik kurumlarda değişiklik - Adalet, Aile ve Sosyal Hizmetler, Sağlık, Hazine ve Maliye ile İçişleri bakanlıklarının da aralarında bulunduğu çok sayıda kamu kurumunun dolu ve boş kadrolarında değişikliğe gidildi. 49 sayfalık Cumhurbaşkanı Kararı, kadroların unvan ve derece cetvellerini yeniden düzenliyor. Kamu kurum ve kuruluşlarının kadro yapısında kapsamlı bir düzenlemeye gidildi. 28 Kasım 2026 tarihli Resmî Gazete'de yayımlanan 2026/413 sayılı Cumhurbaşkanı Kararı ile çok sayıda bakanlık, başkanlık, genel müdürlük ve kamu kurumunun dolu ve boş kadrolarında değişiklik yapıldı. CNBCE.COM'u öncelikli haber kaynağınız olarak ekleyin Ekle Cumhurbaşkanı Recep Tayyip Erdoğan'ın imzasını taşıyan karar, 2 sayılı Genel Kadro ve Usulü Hakkında Cumhurbaşkanlığı Kararnamesi'nin 7'nci maddesi kapsamında yayımlandı. 49 sayfalık ek listede kurumların merkez ve taşra teşkilatları ayrı ayrı ele alındı. Düzenleme kapsamında mevcut kadroların unvanları, adetleri ve dereceleri üzerinden değişiklikler yapıldı. Çok sayıda bakanlık ve kamu kurumu kapsama alındı Karar ekindeki listelerde Adalet Bakanlığı, Aile ve Sosyal Hizmetler Bakanlığı, Çalışma ve Sosyal Güvenlik Bakanlığı, Çevre, Şehircilik ve İklim Değişikliği Bakanlığı, Hazine ve Maliye Bakanlığı, İçişleri Bakanlığı, Kültür ve Turizm Bakanlığı, Sağlık Bakanlığı ve Ticaret Bakanlığı gibi kurumlar yer aldı. Bunların yanı sıra Emniyet Genel Müdürlüğü, Gelir İdaresi Başkanlığı, Devlet Su İşleri Genel Müdürlüğü, Karayolları Genel Müdürlüğü, Tapu ve Kadastro Genel Müdürlüğü, Türkiye İstatistik Kurumu, Danıştay ve Yargıtay da düzenleme kapsamına girdi. Üniversitelerin bazı kadroları da karar ekindeki listelerde yer aldı. Dolu kadrolarda unvan ve derece değişiklikleri Kararın önemli bölümlerinden birini dolu kadro değişiklikleri oluşturdu. Bu bölümde mevcut kadroların unvanları, adetleri ve dereceleri gösterilerek yapılması uygun görülen değişiklikler sıralandı. Örneğin Adalet Bakanlığı'nın merkez ve taşra teşkilatlarında çok sayıda unvana ilişkin kadro düzenlemesi yapıldı. Listelerde hâkim ve savcı yardımcıları dışındaki idari ve teknik kadroların yanı sıra zabıt kâtibi, mübaşir, infaz ve koruma memuru, mühendis, tekniker ve çeşitli uzman unvanları da bulunuyor. Aile ve Sosyal Hizmetler Bakanlığı'nda sosyal çalışmacı, psikolog, çocuk gelişimcisi, hemşire, mühendis ve öğretmen gibi unvanların yer aldığı kadrolar düzenlendi. Sağlık Bakanlığı'nın merkez ve taşra teşkilatlarında da mühendis, tekniker, teknisyen, mimar ve çeşitli idari unvanlardaki kadrolar için değişiklikler öngörüldü. Boş kadrolar da yeniden düzenlendi Kararın bir diğer bölümünde boş kadro değişiklikleri yer aldı. news.title: KİT'lerde büyük kadro düzenlemesi: Çok sayıda yeni pozisyon açıldı, mevcut kadrolar değişti
news.summary: Cumhurbaşkanı kararıyla Eti Maden, TCDD, EÜAŞ, TEİAŞ, DHMİ, TMO ve ÇAYKUR'un da aralarında bulunduğu kamu işletmelerinde kadro ve pozisyon değişikliğine gidildi. Bazı yönetici kadroları kaldırılırken mühendis, tekniker, memur ve teknik uzman pozisyonları oluşturuldu.
news.verification: Editoryal haber; resmî duyuru olarak değerlendirilmemeli
news.titleTr: KİT'lerde büyük kadro düzenlemesi: Çok sayıda yeni pozisyon açıldı, mevcut kadrolar değişti
news.summaryTr: Cumhurbaşkanı kararıyla Eti Maden, TCDD, EÜAŞ, TEİAŞ, DHMİ, TMO ve ÇAYKUR'un da aralarında bulunduğu kamu işletmelerinde kadro ve pozisyon değişikliğine gidildi. Bazı yönetici kadroları kaldırılırken mühendis, tekniker, memur ve teknik uzman pozisyonları oluşturuldu.
news.articleText: KİT'lerde büyük kadro düzenlemesi: Çok sayıda yeni pozisyon açıldı, mevcut kadrolar değişti - Cumhurbaşkanı kararıyla Eti Maden, TCDD, EÜAŞ, TEİAŞ, DHMİ, TMO ve ÇAYKUR'un da aralarında bulunduğu kamu işletmelerinde kadro ve pozisyon değişikliğine gidildi. Bazı yönetici kadroları kaldırılırken mühendis, tekniker, memur ve teknik uzman pozisyonları oluşturuldu. Kamu iktisadi teşebbüsleri ve bağlı ortaklıklarının kadro yapısında değişikliğe gidildi. 28 Kasım 2026 tarihli Resmî Gazete'de yayımlanan 2026/414 sayılı Cumhurbaşkanı Kararı ile çeşitli kamu kurumlarının merkez ve taşra teşkilatlarında bazı kadrolar iptal edilirken yeni kadro ve pozisyonlar ihdas edildi. CNBCE.COM'u öncelikli haber kaynağınız olarak ekleyin Ekle Cumhurbaşkanı Recep Tayyip Erdoğan'ın imzasını taşıyan karar, iki ayrı liste üzerinden düzenlendi. Birinci listede kurumların kadro cetvellerindeki değişiklikler, ikinci listede ise pozisyon cetvellerindeki düzenlemeler yer aldı. Düzenlemeyle birlikte özellikle teknik kadrolar, mühendislik pozisyonları ve taşra teşkilatındaki yönetici kadroları öne çıktı. Eti Maden'de başuzman kadroları kaldırıldı Eti Maden İşletmeleri Genel Müdürlüğü'nün merkez teşkilatında 20 başuzman kadrosu iptal edildi. Bunun karşılığında 5 birim müdür yardımcısı ve 5 müfettiş yardımcısı kadrosu oluşturuldu. Kurumun merkez pozisyonlarında ise 2 şef yardımcısı pozisyonu kaldırılırken 2 teknik uzman ve 2 teknik şef pozisyonu ihdas edildi. Eti Maden'in taşra teşkilatında da değişikliğe gidildi. Üç şef yardımcısı ve bir veznedar pozisyonu kaldırılırken 2 teknik uzman, 1 avukat ve 30 mühendis pozisyonu oluşturuldu. Türkiye Şeker Fabrikaları ve ÇAYKUR'da değişiklik Türkiye Şeker Fabrikaları A.Ş. Genel Müdürlüğü'nün merkez teşkilatında bir müfettiş kadrosunda derece değişikliği yapıldı. Taşra teşkilatında ise 12 kısım müdürü kadrosu oluşturuldu. Kurumun taşra pozisyonlarında 12 uzman pozisyonu iptal edildi. Çay İşletmeleri Genel Müdürlüğü'nün taşra teşkilatında ise 2 bölge müdür yardımcısı ve 1 pazarlama ve üretim bölge müdürü kadrosu kaldırıldı. Böylece toplam 3 kadro iptal edilmiş oldu. EÜAŞ ve TEİAŞ'ta mühendislik ve yönetici pozisyonları Elektrik Üretim A.Ş. (EÜAŞ) Genel Müdürlüğü'nün taşra teşkilatında 10 müdür kadrosu iptal edilirken 1 hukuk müşaviri kadrosu oluşturuldu. EÜAŞ'ın taşra pozisyonlarında da 21 koruma ve güvenlik görevlisi pozisyonu kaldırıldı. Bunun karşılığında 21 mühendis pozisyonu ihdas edildi. Türkiye Elektrik İletim A.Ş. (TEİAŞ) Genel Müdürlüğü'nün merkez teşkilatında 5 müfettiş kadrosu oluşturuldu. Kurumun taşra teşkilatında ise 5 müdür yardımcısı ve 25 başmühendis pozisyonu ihdas edildi. DHMİ'ye 50 tekniker pozisyonu Devlet Hava Meydanları İşletmesi (DHMİ) Genel Müdürlüğü'nün taşra teşkilatında çeşitli yönetici pozisyonları oluşturuldu. Buna göre 2 havacılık acil yardım ve güvenlik müdürü, 10 nöbetçi müdür, 2 başmüdür, 4 başmüdür yardımcısı ve 18 şube müdürü pozisyonu ihdas edildi. Bu düzenlemeyle söz konusu unvanlarda toplam 36 pozisyon oluşturuldu. DHMİ taşra teşkilatında ayrıca 50 tekniker pozisyonu açıldı. TCDD'de gişe memuru pozisyonları değişti TCDD Taşımacılık A.Ş. Genel Müdürlüğü'nün merkez teşkilatında şube müdürü pozisyonlarında derece düzenlemesine gidildi. Bu kapsamda 8 şube müdürü pozisyonu için cetvel değişikliği yapıldı. Kurumun merkez teşkilatında ayrıca 2 tekniker pozisyonu oluşturuldu. Taşra teşkilatında ise 150 gişe memuru pozisyonu iptal edilerek aynı sayıda, yani 150 memur pozisyonu ihdas edildi. Böylece gişe memuru pozisyonları memur pozisyonlarına dönüştürüldü. TMO ve Türkiye Taşkömürü Kurumu'nda düzenleme Toprak Mahsulleri Ofisi (TMO) Genel Müdürlüğü'nün taşra teşkilatında 1 koruma ve güvenlik grup şefi pozisyonu iptal edildi. Aynı cetvelde 45 mühendis pozisyonu oluşturuldu. Türkiye Taşkömürü Kurumu (TTK) Genel Müdürlüğü'nün merkez teşkilatında 20 memur pozisyonu ihdas edildi. Taşra teşkilatında ise 30 koruma ve güvenlik görevlisi pozisyonu iptal edildi.

news.verification: Editoryal haber; resmî duyuru olarak değerlendirilmemeli
news.titleTr: Resmi Gazete'de yayımlandı: Konaklama vergisinde yüzde 1'lik uygulama 2027 sonuna kadar uzatıldı
news.summaryTr: Otel, motel, pansiyon ve tatil köylerini kapsayan konaklama vergisinde indirimli oran uygulaması bir yıl daha devam edecek. Yüzde 1 olarak uygulanan vergi oranı, 31 Aralık 2027'ye kadar geçerli olacak.
news.articleText: Resmi Gazete'de yayımlandı: Konaklama vergisinde yüzde 1'lik uygulama 2027 sonuna kadar uzatıldı - Otel, motel, pansiyon ve tatil köylerini kapsayan konaklama vergisinde indirimli oran uygulaması bir yıl daha devam edecek. Yüzde 1 olarak uygulanan vergi oranı, 31 Aralık 2027'ye kadar geçerli olacak. Konaklama vergisinde indirimli oran uygulamasının süresi uzatıldı. 28 Kasım 2026 tarihli Resmî Gazete'de yayımlanan Cumhurbaşkanı Kararı ile konaklama vergisinin yüzde 1 olarak uygulanmasına ilişkin düzenlemenin süresi 31 Aralık 2027'ye kadar uzatıldı. CNBCE.COM'u öncelikli haber kaynağınız olarak ekleyin Ekle Cumhurbaşkanı Recep Tayyip Erdoğan'ın imzasını taşıyan 12059 sayılı Karar'a göre, 6802 sayılı Gider Vergileri Kanunu'nun 34'üncü maddesinin beşinci fıkrası kapsamında belirlenen vergi oranına ilişkin önceki kararda değişiklik yapıldı. Yüzde 2'den yüzde 1'e indirilmişti Konaklama vergisi oranı, 1 Mayıs 2026 itibarıyla yüzde 2'den yüzde 1'e düşürülmüştü. Yeni kararla indirimli oran uygulamasının 2027 yılı boyunca da sürmesi kararlaştırıldı. Düzenleme; otel, motel, pansiyon ve tatil köyleri gibi konaklama tesislerini kapsıyor. Yeni düzenleme 1 Ocak 2027'de yürürlüğe girecek Karara göre, önceki düzenlemede yer alan 31 Aralık 2026 tarihi, 31 Aralık 2027 olarak değiştirildi. Cumhurbaşkanı Kararı, 1 Ocak 2027 tarihinde yürürlüğe girecek.

news.articleText: TCMB'den Fintix kararı: Elektronik para şirketinin faaliyet izni iptal edildi - TCMB, Fintix Elektronik Para ve Ödeme Hizmetleri A.Ş.’nin faaliyet iznini iptal etti. 27 Kasım tarihli karar, 28 Kasım’da Resmî Gazete’de yayımlandı. Türkiye Cumhuriyet Merkez Bankası (TCMB), Fintix Elektronik Para ve Ödeme Hizmetleri A.Ş.’nin faaliyet izninin iptal edilmesine karar verdi. CNBCE.COM'u öncelikli haber kaynağınız olarak ekleyin Ekle 28 Kasım 2026 tarihli Resmî Gazete’de yayımlanan karara göre, 27 Kasım 2026 tarihli ve 12127/21726 sayılı kararla şirketin faaliyet izni iptal edildi. Faaliyet izni 2024'te verilmişti Fintix Elektronik Para ve Ödeme Hizmetleri A.Ş.’ye, TCMB’nin 17 Ekim 2024 tarihli ve 11727/21326 sayılı kararıyla elektronik para kuruluşu olarak faaliyette bulunma izni verilmişti. Merkez Bankası, 6493 sayılı Ödeme ve Menkul Kıymet Mutabakat Sistemleri, Ödeme Hizmetleri ve Elektronik Para Kuruluşları Hakkında Kanun’un 16’ncı maddesinin birinci fıkrasının (b) bendi ve 19’uncu maddesi uyarınca şirketin faaliyet izninin iptal edilmesine karar verdi. Resmî Gazete’de yayımlanan kararda, faaliyet izninin iptal edilme gerekçesine ilişkin ayrıca bir açıklama yapılmadı.

news.title: SPK'dan 5 hisseye 2 yıl işlem yasağı: Tera grubuna da yasak geldi, 26 fon açılıyor
news.summary: Sermaye Piyasası Kurulu, SKYLP, PASEU, BIGEN, PEKGY ve TERA paylarında yapılan işlemler nedeniyle 2 yıl süreyle işlem yasağı kararı aldı. Beş hissede toplam 167 kişi kaydı bulunurken bazı isimler birden fazla hissede yer aldı.
news.verification: Editoryal haber; resmî duyuru olarak değerlendirilmemeli
news.titleTr: SPK'dan 5 hisseye 2 yıl işlem yasağı: Tera grubuna da yasak geldi, 26 fon açılıyor
news.summaryTr: Sermaye Piyasası Kurulu, SKYLP, PASEU, BIGEN, PEKGY ve TERA paylarında yapılan işlemler nedeniyle 2 yıl süreyle işlem yasağı kararı aldı. Beş hissede toplam 167 kişi kaydı bulunurken bazı isimler birden fazla hissede yer aldı.
news.articleText: SPK'dan 5 hisseye 2 yıl işlem yasağı: Tera grubuna da yasak geldi, 26 fon açılıyor - Sermaye Piyasası Kurulu, SKYLP, PASEU, BIGEN, PEKGY ve TERA paylarında yapılan işlemler nedeniyle 2 yıl süreyle işlem yasağı kararı aldı. Beş hissede toplam 167 kişi kaydı bulunurken bazı isimler birden fazla hissede yer aldı. Sermaye Piyasası Kurulu (SPK), 27 Kasım 2026 tarihli bülteninde sermaye piyasalarına yönelik bir dizi karar açıkladı. SKYLP, PASEU, BIGEN, PEKGY ve TERA pay piyasalarındaki işlemler nedeniyle kişi ve kurumlar hakkında 2 yıl süreyle borsalarda işlem yapma yasağı uygulanmasına karar verildi. CNBCE.COM'u öncelikli haber kaynağınız olarak ekleyin Ekle Bültendeki listelerde beş hisse için toplam 167 kişi kaydı bulunuyor. Bazı isimlerin birden fazla hisseye ilişkin listelerde yer alması nedeniyle bu rakam, tekilleştirilmiş kişi sayısını göstermiyor. Hisse bazında işlem yasağı listeleri SPK bültenindeki listelere göre işlem yasağı getirilen kişi kayıtlarının hisse bazında dağılımı şöyle: - SKYLP: 14 kişi - PASEU: 20 kişi - BIGEN: 58 kişi - PEKGY: 26 kişi - TERA: 49 kişi Tera grubu şirketlerine 2 yıl işlem yasağı SPK kararlarında Tera grubuna bağlı şirketler için de hisse bazında işlem yasakları yer aldı. - Tera Portföy Yönetimi: TERA, BIGEN ve PEKGY paylarında kendi nam ve hesabına gerçekleştirdiği işlemlerle sınırlı olmak üzere yasak kapsamına alındı. - Tera Yatırım Bankası: BIGEN ve PEKGY paylarında kendi nam ve hesabına gerçekleştirdiği işlemlerle sınırlı olarak işlem yasağı getirildi. - Tera Yatırım Holding: PEKGY pay piyasasındaki işlemler kapsamında 2 yıl işlem yasağı kararı verildi. - Hedef Portföy Yönetimi: BIGEN pay piyasasında kendi nam ve hesabına gerçekleştirdiği işlemlerle sınırlı olmak üzere yasak kapsamına alındı. Suç duyurusu listelerinde dikkat çeken isimler SPK'nın suç duyurusunda bulunulmasına karar verdiği listelerde Bülent Uygun, Emre Alkin, Emre Tezmen, Erkan Kilimci ve Ali Hepşen gibi isimler de yer aldı. Kurul ayrıca SKYLP, PASEU, BIGEN, PEKGY ve TERA pay piyasalarındaki işlemler nedeniyle hakkında suç duyurusu kararı verilen bazı kişilerin sahip oldukları tüm sermaye piyasası lisanslarının, işlem yasağı süresince iptal edilmesine karar verdi. Suç duyurusu kararı, kişiler hakkında verilmiş bir mahkûmiyet kararı anlamına gelmiyor. Söz konusu karar, SPK'nın ilgili işlemler nedeniyle adli makamlara başvurma yönündeki kararını ifade ediyor. 26 fon yeniden işleme açılıyor SPK bülteninin fon yatırımcılarını ilgilendiren önemli kararlarından biri de 17 Eylül 2026'da alım satıma kapatılan fonlara ilişkin oldu. Kurul, TEFAS'ta ve TEFAS dışındaki dağıtım kanallarında işlemleri durdurulan toplam 26 fonun, 30 Kasım 2026 Pazartesi günü eş zamanlı olarak yeniden alım satıma açılabilmesine karar verdi. Yeniden işleme açılacak fonlar arasında Bulls Portföy'e ait 9 fon ile A1 Capital Portföy ve Pardus Portföy tarafından yönetilen 17 fon bulunuyor.

items.title: 'I don't know what I'd do without it': Why shoppers and staff fear losing Poundland
items.summary: The discount retailer has collapsed into administration after its US owners failed to secure a rescue deal.
items.verification: Editoryal haber; resmî duyuru olarak değerlendirilmemeli
items.titleTr: 'I don't know what I'd do without it': Why shoppers and staff fear losing Poundland
items.summaryTr: The discount retailer has collapsed into administration after its US owners failed to secure a rescue deal.
items.articleText: 'I don't know what I'd do without it': Why shoppers and staff fear losing Poundland - Published For Charlie Franklyn, a trip to Poundland is almost as routine as going to work. The care worker from Teesside pops into her local branch nearly every day – it's where she buys cleaning products, beauty bargains and the budget-friendly finds she loves sharing online. Charlie has been creating social media content for five years, and Poundland is one of her regular filming spots. Her videos showcasing the store and its wares have proved popular, and although she's never been paid by the retailer, she's been gifted products over the years and built relationships with staff who invite her in to film. "For me, Poundland is more than just a shopping stop. I buy so many things from there that are much cheaper than in other shops." 'We don't need empty shops on the high street' The budget retailer has gone into administration, putting 11,000 jobs at risk in the run-up to Christmas. For now, its 600 stores continue to trade as usual but they will eventually close if a buyer can't be found to rescue some or all of the business. Charlie says she was "surprised by the news" and is worried about what it could mean for shoppers like her. "With the cost-of-living crisis going on, places like Poundland are so important and we really don't need empty shops on the high street," she tells the BBC. "I don't know what I'll do without it." Other shoppers the BBC spoke to are equally concerned. Kimi Browne, 26, from London, doesn't often shop at Poundland but relies on it for seasonal bargains, including Halloween decorations and accessories for her clothes. She says the retailer is "an important part of the community as it offers affordable products for families". Rea Catedrilla has a friend who works at the Poundland store in Notting Hill and feels "sad and sorry" for those who could lose their jobs. She visits Poundland around four times per week because "it's less expensive than other shops and it's very convenient". Poundland opened its first store in Burton-upon-Trent in 1990 and grew into one of the UK's best-known discount retailers, with 900 shops across the country at its peak. But rising costs and competition from supermarkets such as Aldi and Lidl put pressure on the business and, in June 2025, it was sold to US investment firm Gordon Brothers for a nominal £1. There had been signs of a recovery – Poundland made a profit of £18.1m in the year to September, compared with a £68m loss the previous year. But Gordon Brothers insists the business has missed its budget forecasts and would continue to struggle even if only its worst-performing stores were closed. News of the administration has left many Poundland staff on edge. Aboud, 39, who manages the Camden branch in north London, says it feels like a "slap in the face", as he thought the chain had started to recover over the last 18 months. "Everything we've worked hard for was for nothing. Someone has come in and dismantled all that effort." Aboud says his colleagues at the store have been emotional and that it's "very worrying to have a job at risk given the current climate". But he adds that his team "are still hopeful" that a buyer could rescue the chain and that they continue to give "100% regardless of the circumstances". 'Yesterday's business' Retail expert Mary Portas said that when Poundland first opened, it was "everything under one roof that you didn't even know you wanted or needed" but it failed to keep pace as the market evolved. While inflation has made it harder to sustain the £1 pricing model, other discount retailers have also made value shopping a more appealing experience, she says. "Value brands, instead of looking shabby, which quite frankly Poundland often did, have taken themselves into a much better place," she says. "On so many levels, Poundland just felt like yesterday's business." The company has now appointed consultancy AlixPartners to oversee a sale of part or all of the discount retailer. Administrators will decide whether to sell the business as a whole or break it up, with the latter considered the more likely outcome. Helen Howes, Poundland's store manager in Camborne, Cornwall, says she wishes staff "could have been told more at times". She adds that losing Poundland would be "devastating" for the town as it's one of its larger shops and an important draw for shoppers. Jilly, who shops at the branch in Ealing, says the store has been a "godsend" and that it would be a blow to the local community if it closed. Her shopping trolley is filled with everything from cleaning products and stationery to "upmarket things that I will gift for Christmas". "It's tragic, everyone losing their jobs just before Christmas," she adds. Additional reporting by Emma Simpson. Related topics - Published1 day ago - Published1 day ago - Published1 day ago

items.summaryTr: The Canadian man, who pleaded guilty to 14 counts of aiding and abetting suicide earlier this year, said he was remorseful for his actions.
items.articleText: 'Poison seller' Kenneth Law apologises in court to the families of his victims - Published The Canadian man who sold toxic chemicals through online suicide forums in 40 countries apologised in court to the families of the victims, saying he deeply regrets his actions and will never repeat them. Kenneth Law made the remarks on Friday during a sentencing hearing where prosecutors asked a judge to give him a 25-year prison term. The 61-year-old pleaded guilty in May to 14 counts of aiding the suicide deaths of 14 people in Ontario, Canada, though he has admitted to causing the deaths of dozens of victims in England and Wales. He will not face charges in the UK or over any British deaths under a plea deal which saw Canadian authorities withdraw more serious charges of murder. During Friday's sentencing hearing in an Ontario court, prosecutors stressed that many of his victims were young and struggling with mental distress. If Law receives the prosecution's recommended sentence, he would serve just under 20 years in prison, after accounting for credit for time served since his May 2023 arrest. As she sought to make her case in court on Friday, Crown Attorney Kathleen Doherty described Law as a predator taking advantage of "vulnerable people". "What they needed was help. But what they found was Mr Law and his products for death," Doherty said. She also said Law's motives were financial. "If people could pay, he sold it to them. There's no discussion or inquiries or anything going on whereby Mr Law would have any ability to appreciate the circumstances of the individual he was dealing with," she said. Law's defence lawyer, Matthew Gourlay, countered those claims, arguing that his client was not responsible for any of their battles with mental illness.. "Each of these incidents is its own unique tragedy," Gourlay said. items.articleText: The Indian 'Tamasha queen' whose fans paid for a show that never happened - Published Few things could keep Vithabai Narayangaonkar, one of the greatest stars of Maharashtra's folk theatre, away from the stage. Not even, it would seem, the birth of her child. In the 1960s, the singer, dancer and troupe leader was performing in Shikhar Shingnapur, a village in the western Indian state, when she went into labour. "She quietly stepped behind the stage into a makeshift tent while the rest of us continued performing," her daughter, veteran folk artist Mangala Bansode, told BBC Marathi. Outside, the restless audience kept shouting: "Where is Vitha?" When Vithabai returned to the stage, she was cradling her newborn son, the seventh of her eight children. "The audience was stunned, but they quietly left, saying, 'We will watch your performance later'," Bansode recalled. Outspoken and quick-witted, Vithabai held audiences across Maharashtra in thrall for decades, earning the title of Tamasha Samradnyi – the empress of Tamasha, the state's traditional travelling folk theatre. Now, more than two decades after her death, her life has inspired a Bollywood musical, Eetha, starring Shraddha Kapoor, and due for release on 4 December. Directed by Laxman Utekar, Eetha is based on Yogiraj Bagul's Marathi book chronicling Vithabai's life. Rooted in devotional poetry, Tamasha evolved into a lively mix of music, dance, comedy and drama. At its heart is Lavani, a song and dance tradition in which verses ranging from the bawdy to the politically incisive are performed to the beat of the dholki, a percussion instrument. Eetha evokes the world of Tamasha in its heyday. Kapoor, who had never performed Lavani before, learnt to dance while wearing musical anklets weighing 4kg each. "The lives of Tamasha artists have been very tough, so in their dance you see pain as well as joy," Kapoor recalled at a promotional event. Many Tamasha performers, including Vithabai, came from oppressed castes, facing discrimination even as their artistry drew large crowds. How much of that history Eetha will capture remains debated. Utekar says it is not a biopic, but his decision to rename the protagonist Vithabai Bhau Gavkar instead of Vithabai Bhau Mang Narayangaonkar has drawn criticism. For critics, much of Vithabai's history was contained in her name – Mang identified her with a historically oppressed Dalit community, while Narayangaonkar spoke of her family's roots in Narayangaon village. Both featured in the name of the troupe she inherited from her father – Bhau-Bapu Mang Narayangaonkar Tamasha Mandal. Vithabai spoke openly about caste and the indignities Tamasha artists faced, themes that also surfaced in her songs. In a 1960s Lavani documented by historian Shailaja Paik, she rebuked men for lewd gestures, reminding them she danced to earn a living, not to please them. It was a livelihood she had inherited from generations of performers in her family. Like her son, Vithabai was born during a Tamasha performance, in 1935. Her mother, Shanta, had continued touring with her husband Bhau's troupe throughout her pregnancy. Vithabai joined a theatre group at eight and her father's troupe at 13, soon becoming its star. After her father and co-leader Bapu died in quick succession, she took over the troupe with her husband and cousin. Her career flourished during Tamasha's golden age, when productions grew more elaborate, drawing on mythology, history and contemporary life, says folk arts scholar Sukhada Khandge. Khandge, who watched Vithabai perform as a child, recalls her sparkling eyes and commanding presence. She was as expressive with her face as she was with her feet. Her fame carried her beyond Maharashtra. During India's war with China in 1962, Vithabai performed for soldiers in the North-East Frontier Agency, now largely Arunachal Pradesh, braving freezing conditions just three months after giving birth, Bansode says. At a conference in 1996, she recalled meeting soldiers from the historically oppressed Mahar and Mang communities at the frontier. "Our Mahar-Mang soldiers were expected to fight and lay down their lives defending the nation, but the very same people would not even allow our bridegroom to pass through the village entrance," she said. Despite offers from leading filmmakers, including Raj Kapoor, and roles in Marathi cinema, Vithabai refused to leave theatre. Film fame, she felt, would benefit her alone, while her troupe supported some 50 families, Bansode says. There was a tenderness, too, in her relationship with audiences. In his book on Vithabai's life, which inspired Eetha, Yogiraj Bagul recounts a performance in Mumbai during Diwali in 1971. Despite the threat of rain, spectators insisted on buying tickets, saying the money would be their Bhau Beej gift to Vithabai if the show was cancelled – a festival celebrating the bond between brothers and sisters. When the rain came, people left chanting: "Bhau Beej, Bhau Beej." No one asked for their money back. But Vithabai's fortunes failed to match her fame. Her husband, Maruti Sawant, mismanaged the troupe's finances and took loans in her name, family members say. By the time she left him in 1982, she was heavily indebted. Bagul also writes about a 1986 column in a Marathi daily that revealed how the empress of Tamasha was now travelling on public buses and staying in cheap accommodation. Despite public support, Vithabai was forced to disband her troupe in 1990 – the same year she received the Sangeet Natak Akademi Award, one of India's highest performing arts honours. Vithabai successfully campaigned for government pensions for Tamasha artists. But many of the hardships she knew persist today, says Marathi writer Pradnya Daya Pawar. Troupes spend nearly eight months a year on the road, with performers struggling to feed their children and educate them, she says. Despite government aid, many remain indebted to private moneylenders. Vithabai's financial struggles persisted until her death in January 2002. Her family could pay only 4,000 of the 5,900 rupees owed to the Pune hospital where she died, the Times of India reported. Fellow artists and admirers chipped in to bring her body home to Narayangaon. Maharashtra has since instituted a lifetime achievement award in her name. Eetha could now introduce Vithabai to a generation that never saw her perform, though the changes to her name have left some uneasy. Marathi writer Pragya Daya Pawar argues that omitting the reference to Vithabai's caste risks obscuring the difficulties she confronted. "It erases the social location, struggle and resistance that shaped her remarkable journey, reducing an extraordinary artist's story to a purely individual achievement," she says. But Bansode, who spent years performing alongside her mother, says there is much to celebrate. "The name doesn't matter to me. I am simply proud that a film is being made about my mother," she says.

items.titleTr: A clinic is reassessing people with ADHD and autism diagnoses - but critics fear it could deepen stigma
items.summaryTr: While many people find a diagnosis for ADHD or autism affirming, a government-funded clinic in Sweden is re-assessing people who feel it does not reflect them.
items.articleText: A clinic is reassessing people with ADHD and autism diagnoses - but critics fear it could deepen stigma - Published Freya looks nervous as she walks into a psychiatric clinic in Sweden for an ADHD assessment. Countries around the world have seen a huge increase in ADHD diagnoses over recent decades. For many people this can be life changing, helping them understand themselves better and access support. But Freya (not her real name) is not attending a long-awaited appointment to secure a diagnosis. This government-funded clinic offers autism and ADHD diagnosis reassessments - its doctors believe it is the first in the world dedicated solely to this purpose. At 12, Freya was struggling with anxiety at school and sought out professional help. "They thought I had ADHD," she says. But as she grew up, she felt that she did not experience ADHD symptoms. "I don't think I had it in the first place," she now says. Her doubts about the diagnosis became more pressing as a teenager, when she discovered that in Sweden, it could be a barrier to pursuing her dream career of joining the police. "I want to have every option open," she tells BBC World Service. If the doctors at the clinic decide Freya does not meet the ADHD criteria, her medical records will be updated, and it will be easier for her to apply for a job with the police. The clinic, known as Mottagning Neuropsykiatri, has opened at a time when rates of ADHD and autism diagnoses are under the spotlight. Many say this is because of greater awareness of the symptoms, and that previously neglected groups - particularly women and girls - are finally getting the diagnoses they need, while others argue that the growing numbers stem from overdiagnosis. The existence of the clinic is controversial. Clinical guidance from UK governing bodies and the World Health Organization describe autism as a lifelong condition and ADHD as a neurodevelopmental condition that can persist into adulthood. The medical consensus is that both diagnoses last a lifetime, even if symptoms fluctuate. And some neurodiversity advocates warn that a dedicated reassessment service could reinforce the idea that being diagnosed with ADHD or autism is undesirable – and deepen the stigma surrounding both conditions. Despite this, hundreds of people have approached the clinic about reassessment. Barred from jobs Like Freya, other young adults have been prompted to reconsider their diagnosis after they felt it had become a barrier. This is because historically, Swedes with ADHD or autism were barred from certain jobs, including joining the military, and becoming police officers, train drivers and pilots. This is despite research suggesting some neurodivergent traits can be strengths in certain roles. No such bans exist in the UK, although rules differ globally. Since 2022, people with ADHD have been able to join the Swedish military if they are medication-free. And since 2021, people with ADHD or autism have been able to apply to join the police, but must submit a medical certificate, which can cost around 15,000 SEK (£1,100) privately. When Freya was referred to the clinic, she says she was relieved to find out she could get her diagnosis reassessed there for free. Johanna, 24, was diagnosed with ADHD at 14 after what she describes as a period of bad behaviour at school. She found the diagnosis helpful at first and received additional support from teachers. But as she grew into adulthood, she says she stopped feeling that she needed extra support. And after discovering it was a barrier to becoming a police officer, she began questioning whether it was even accurate. Johanna says she has some traits of ADHD, such as a short attention span, "but not enough to have an ADHD diagnosis," she believes. Johanna was reassessed aged 21 during an early pilot of the reassessment clinic and was found not to meet its diagnostic criteria for ADHD. She now works for her father's company, and does not plan on becoming a police officer. What is an ADHD or autism reassessment? Both ADHD and autism are neurodevelopmental conditions that affect how people think and interact with the world. They are diagnosed through detailed assessments, which can include questionnaires and interviews, rather than one single clinical test. The doctors at Mottagning Neuropsykiatri say their approach is different from traditional assessments, as it focuses less on someone's history, and more on the symptoms they are experiencing in the present. "This is not de-diagnosing, this is a renewed assessment of your functioning today," says Sebastian Lundström, the clinic's lead psychologist. The doctors say they do not judge whether the original assessment was correct, so rather than wiping the original diagnosis from patients' medical records, they add a note of the new assessment. Lundström says that some people who once had a diagnosis but are found to not meet the criteria at the clinic may have been misdiagnosed. But he also believes that for a small minority, ADHD and autism are not lifelong conditions and individuals may stop experiencing symptoms as they grow older. But updating a person's diagnosis because they are not currently showing symptoms is a contested approach. "We have to remember that these are lifelong conditions," says Navid Ghannad, chair of Autism Skåne, a local Swedish non-profit for autistic people and their families. "Because at a certain point in their adulthood during a clinical setting they have had their diagnosis removed, it doesn't necessarily mean that the ADHD or the autism has disappeared," he adds. Symptoms could reappear later in life, he says. "The problem is once they resurface, that individual which doesn't have a diagnosis any longer, they will not be able to get the timely and correct support." Lundström says he does not consider it a big risk that people could get reassessed and find themselves without necessary support. During the pilot he encountered people who "really wanted" to get rid of their diagnosis but the psychologist said, "we still feel that you meet the criteria". 'I was stuck' Vilda, 22, sought reassessment of her autism diagnosis which was initially given after she experienced a trauma. "I didn't recognise myself in the description of autism," she says. "I was stuck. I know that this is not me, but I can't do anything about it." It was requests from people like Johanna and Vilda that led to the establishment of the clinic, Lundström explains. "It gained momentum by itself and the word spread around. A lot of people contacted us and we felt that there was a justification for starting up," he says. It is only open one day a month. Before opening the clinic, Lundström conducted a small peer-reviewed study - of the 72 individuals who took part, roughly 80% did not meet the criteria for ADHD or autism. All the participants already wanted to lose their diagnosis, rather than being a randomly selected group. "It's important to stress that this patient population is not necessarily representative for all with autism and ADHD," he adds. During the first year of the pilot some 400 to 500 people spoke to Lundström, who is also associate professor of child and adolescent psychiatric sciences at the University of Gothenburg, about getting a reassessment. The project also has the backing of senior figures in Swedish psychiatry, including Sophia Eberhard, a senior consultant specialising in child and adolescent psychiatry. "It's psychiatry who in the beginning made those diagnoses," she says. "I believe we have a responsibility to help these young adults on their way." In September, the BBC was given permission to join Freya as she became the first patient to attend the newly opened clinic, which serves both men and women. During her appointment, Freya takes part in questionnaires and verbal assessments to see if she meets the ADHD criteria. The process is the same for both ADHD and autism, although the questions differ. Freya says she is hopeful that she will be able to "get rid" of her ADHD diagnosis after the appointment. But the doctors are adamant that they do not just give attendees the outcome they want. They conduct other checks such as assessing body language and communication skills, speaking to younger patients' parents, and checking medical files for ongoing treatment. Fears about stigma The opening of the clinic has drawn criticism from those who fear it sends the wrong message about autism and ADHD. "The clinic presents neurodiversity and autistic people as a bad thing, like we are a problem that needs to be fixed - we are not," says Jenny Hedin, from charity Organiserade Autister Västernorrland, an advocacy organisation run by and for autistic adults. Hedin, who is autistic and has ADHD, warns that people who can successfully "mask" or mimic neurotypical behaviour might feel under pressure to lose their diagnosis in order to be better accepted by society. "That is especially a problem with women and girls, because girls are usually great at masking," she adds. Others say the focus should be on changing the rules that make it difficult for people with ADHD or autism to pursue certain careers. Eric Donell, the chairman of Riksförbundet Attention, a national Swedish charity, lobbies to remove employment restrictions affecting neurodivergent people, which he says are unfair. He stresses that for many people, getting a diagnosis is extremely important. "Instead of asking people to get rid of their diagnosis, sometimes we should just ask whether the rules themselves are justified," he says. Reassessments risk becoming "a way of adapting the individual to society instead of adapting society to human differences," he adds. 'Magic spell' People from the UK, Denmark, Norway and Germany have also been in touch for reassessment, says Lundström, but they have been turned away, as the clinic only serves locals. Georgina, 35, from the UK, contacted the clinic because she wants to have the autism diagnosis she received at 25 "removed". "It felt like a magic spell, that I'd get this label and the world would be more understanding," she says. Instead, she says, her colleagues belittled her. Georgina has since been offered an NHS reassessment. The process is the same as the original assessment she went through, and can result in patients receiving more diagnoses, fewer diagnoses or no change. The Swedish reassessment clinic says they generally would not apply new or additional diagnoses to people - something Georgina was attracted to. "The situation where you can go in and then come out with other labels... that's really off-putting," she says. For now, she has decided not to undergo an NHS reassessment. Instead, she is trying to find out how often a diagnosis is reconsidered, before deciding whether to go ahead. Back in Sweden, a few hours after Freya entered the clinic, she re-emerges from a consultation room. The doctors here have found that, right now, she does not meet the criteria for an ADHD diagnosis. She says it is "confirmation" that she was right to question her diagnosis. "Now, finally, I have the same opportunity as everyone else."
